title: The 70/30 wardrobe rule: both meanings, with examples
h1: The 70/30 wardrobe rule, explained: basics vs trends and neutrals vs colour
excerpt: The 70/30 wardrobe rule has two common meanings: basics vs trend pieces, and neutrals vs colour. How each works, how to count your ratio and adjust it.
tldr: The 70/30 wardrobe rule says about 70% of your clothes should be versatile and 30% should add personality. It means either 70% basics to 30% trend pieces, or 70% neutrals to 30% colour and pattern. Pick one meaning, count your pieces and adjust gradually.
body:
The 70/30 wardrobe rule says roughly 70% of your clothes should be versatile pieces that go with almost everything, and about 30% should be pieces that add personality. People use it in two overlapping ways: 70% timeless basics to 30% trend pieces, or 70% neutral colours to 30% colours and prints. Both aim for the same result, a wardrobe where most things work together and every bold piece has something to pair with.

What is the 70/30 wardrobe rule?

It's a rule of thumb, not a formal method. There's no single documented creator; it circulates through stylists, fashion writers and capsule wardrobe guides, and the percentages are approximate. Here are the two meanings you'll come across.

Meaning 1: basics vs trend pieces

About 70% of your wardrobe is classic, versatile pieces that won't date quickly: straight-leg jeans, plain T-shirts, a navy jumper, a trench or wool coat, white trainers. The other 30% is trend-led or expressive: this year's cut, a bold print, a statement jacket.

The point is spending. Basics get worn for years, so most of your money goes there, while trends get a smaller, capped share. If a trend passes, you've lost a few pieces, not your whole wardrobe.

Meaning 2: neutrals vs colour and pattern

About 70% of your wardrobe is in neutral colours: black, white, grey, navy, beige, camel, olive, denim blue. The other 30% is colour and pattern: a cobalt shirt, a striped top, a green coat, a floral dress.

The point here is pairing. A rust-coloured jumper is easy to wear if you own four neutral bottoms to put it with. Five patterned shirts and one pair of plain trousers is where "nothing to wear" comes from.

Where the two meanings disagree

Most of the time they overlap, but not always. A classic piece can be colourful, and a trend piece can be neutral:

PieceBasics vs trendsNeutrals vs colour
Navy chinosBasicNeutral
White oxford shirtBasicNeutral
Cobalt-blue crew-neck jumperBasic (a classic shape)Colour
Beige barrel-leg jeansTrend (a cut that may date)Neutral
Leopard-print scarfStatementPattern

Pick one meaning before you count. If you're trying to shop less wastefully, use basics vs trends. If you're struggling to put outfits together, use neutrals vs colour.

The 70/30 outfit rule

The same ratio also gets applied to a single outfit: about 70% of what you're wearing forms a calm base, and about 30% is the accent. Navy trousers, a white shirt and a grey jumper make the base; green trainers and a rust scarf are the accent. Some stylists apply it to texture instead, such as smooth cotton and wool for the base with one chunky knit or suede piece for contrast.

It's a useful check when an outfit feels either flat or busy. Flat usually means 100% base. Busy usually means two or three pieces competing to be the accent.

How to work out your own 70/30 ratio

  1. Decide what to count. Main garments, shoes and outerwear. Leave out underwear, socks, sleepwear and gym clothes, which skew the count without affecting your outfits.
  2. Choose your meaning. Basics vs trends, or neutrals vs colour.
  3. Sort into two groups. Lay everything out, or work through photos. If you can't decide in a few seconds, put the piece with the group it gets worn with least, and move on.
  4. Divide. Pieces in the versatile group ÷ total pieces × 100.

Say you count 50 pieces and 38 are neutral or basic: 38 ÷ 50 = 76%, so you're at roughly 76/24. Close enough. Anything between about 60/40 and 80/20 is within the spirit of the rule.

A digital wardrobe can speed up the counting. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet; when it opens, it will tag each piece you photograph by colour and pattern, which makes a neutral-versus-statement count quicker.

If you're far from 70/30

Mostly basics (85% or more)

Everything matches, but outfits can start to feel like a uniform. You don't need a big shop to fix it:

  • Start with accessories and shoes. A coloured bag, bright trainers or a patterned scarf adds colour to dozens of outfits at once.
  • Try muted colours before loud ones. Sage, rust, burgundy or dusty blue sit easily next to neutrals.
  • Add one statement piece per season, not five at once, and check it works with at least three things you own.

Mostly statement pieces (50% or more)

Each piece looks great on its own, but they fight each other, and getting dressed takes longer than it should.

  • Pause buying colour and print until you've added plain bottoms and simple tops that go with what you already own.
  • Before buying the next printed shirt, count how many plain bottoms it would pair with. Fewer than two is a warning.
  • Look at which statement pieces you actually wear. Keep those, and let the ones that never get worn go.

The 70/30 split describes pieces, not money. Basics often cost less each, but they're also the pieces worth buying in better quality, because they get worn the most. Our guide to the 30 wears rule is a good filter for those purchases.

70/30, 80/20 or 60/40?

You'll see other splits too. They're the same idea with a different dial setting:

SplitFeels likeSuits
80/20Streamlined, close to a uniformStrict dress codes, very small capsules, people who want minimal decisions
70/30Mostly mix-and-match, with room for personalityMost everyday wardrobes
60/40More colour and character, still groundedPeople who love colour and are happy to plan outfits a little more

Pick the split that matches how you dress now, then nudge it. Moving from 50/50 to 70/30 changes how easily outfits come together more than fine-tuning 70/30 to 75/25 ever will. The French phrase moins mais mieux, "less but better", sums up the attitude behind all of these ratios.

The 70/30 rule is one of several numbered wardrobe guidelines; our overview of capsule wardrobe rules compares them. For the versatile 70% itself, the capsule wardrobe essentials checklist is a practical place to start, and the most common traps are in capsule wardrobe mistakes, including going so neutral that you stop enjoying what you wear.

faq.q: What is the 70/30 rule for wardrobe?
faq.a: It's a rule of thumb that about 70% of your clothes should be versatile pieces and about 30% should add personality. It's used in two ways: 70% timeless basics to 30% trend pieces, or 70% neutral colours to 30% colours and prints. Either way, most of your wardrobe mixes and matches, so bolder pieces always have something to pair with.

faq.q: What does 70/30 mean in an outfit?
faq.a: Applied to one outfit, it means about 70% of what you're wearing forms a calm base and about 30% is the accent. For example, navy trousers, a white shirt and a grey jumper as the base, with green trainers and a rust scarf as the accent. Some stylists use it for texture too, pairing smooth fabrics with one chunky or textured piece.

faq.q: Is the 70/30 rule about colour or trends?
faq.a: Both meanings are in use. One version splits your wardrobe into classic basics and trend pieces, which helps you spend wisely. The other splits it into neutral colours and bolder colours or prints, which helps outfits come together. They overlap but can disagree: a cobalt jumper is a basic but not a neutral. Choose one meaning before counting.

faq.q: What is the difference between the 70/30 and 80/20 wardrobe rules?
faq.a: They're the same idea with different proportions. The 80/20 version keeps a larger share of basics or neutrals and feels closer to a uniform, which suits strict dress codes or very small capsule wardrobes. The 70/30 split leaves more room for colour, pattern and trends. Neither is correct; pick the one that matches how you like to dress.

faq.q: How do I work out my wardrobe ratio?
faq.a: Count your main clothes, shoes and outerwear, leaving out underwear, sleepwear and gym kit. Sort each piece into versatile or statement using one meaning of the rule, then divide the versatile count by the total and multiply by 100. For example, 38 versatile pieces out of 50 gives 76%, a ratio of about 76/24.
